title: Flip and multiply, and pigeonhole
summary: Turn dividing by a fraction into an easy multiplication, then prove two things must match whenever there are more things than categories.

problems.prompt: About how many grains of rice are in a 1 kilogram bag of rice?
explanation: Guess and round: estimate with easy numbers first, one part at a time.
A single grain of rice weighs about one fiftieth of a gram, so about 50 grains make up one gram.
A bag holds about 1,000 grams.
50 x 1,000 is 50,000, so about 50,000 grains is the closest guess.
problems.useAgain: when a real count is too big to do one at a time, so you break it into easy parts and multiply.
hints: Think about how many grains fit in a single gram, not the whole bag at once.
Multiply the grains in one gram by the number of grams in the bag.
problems.socraticHint: Why is guessing the number of grains in one gram so much easier than guessing it for the whole bag at once?

variant.prompt: About how many grains of rice are in a 2 kilogram bag of rice?

problems.prompt: About how many times does a kid's heart beat during a full week of sleep, if it beats about 60 times a minute while asleep and a kid sleeps about 10 hours a night?
explanation: Guess and round: 60 beats a minute is 3,600 beats an hour.
10 hours of sleep a night is 3,600 x 10, which is 36,000 beats a night.
Over 7 nights, 36,000 x 7 is about 250,000 beats for the whole week.
problems.useAgain: when a rate needs to scale up through minutes, then hours, then days, one step at a time.
hints: Find beats per hour first, then beats per night, then beats per week.
Round each step before moving to the next multiplication.
problems.socraticHint: Does it matter whether you multiply the three numbers, minutes, hours and nights, in this order or a different order?

variant.prompt: About how many times does a kid's heart beat during a full week of sleep, if it beats about 70 times a minute while asleep and a kid sleeps about 9 hours a night?

problems.prompt: About how many blades of grass are on a soccer field?
explanation: Guess and round: a soccer field covers about 6,000 square meters, round that to 6,000.
Each square meter of grass holds about 1,000 blades, round that to 1,000.
6,000 x 1,000 is 6,000,000, so about 6,000,000 blades is the closest guess.
problems.useAgain: when a whole area is covered in tiny repeated things and you need a rough total.
hints: Think about the size of the whole field in square meters, then blades in one square meter.
Multiply the area of the field by how many blades grow in each square meter.
problems.socraticHint: Which is easier to picture clearly: the whole soccer field at once, or just one square meter of it?

variant.prompt: About how many blades of grass are in a backyard lawn about 60 square meters big?

problems.prompt: A library adds about 15 new books every school day. About how many new books does it add over 4 full school years?
explanation: Guess and round: 15 books a day times about 180 school days a year is 2,700 books a year.
Over 4 years, 2,700 x 4 is 10,800 books.
That rounds to about 11,000 new books over the 4 years.
problems.useAgain: when a daily rate needs to scale up through a school year and then through several years.
hints: Find one year's worth of new books before multiplying by the number of years.
180 school days a year is a good round number to use.
problems.socraticHint: Once you know how many books one year adds, is the multi-year total just one more multiplication away?

variant.prompt: A library adds about 20 new books every school day. About how many new books does it add over 5 full school years?

problems.prompt: About how many bricks make up the outside walls of a small brick house?
explanation: Guess and round: a wall might be about 20 rows of bricks tall, round that to 20.
Each row might run about 50 bricks long, round that to 50.
The house has about 4 main outside walls, round that to 4.
20 x 50 x 4 is 4,000, so about 4,000 bricks is the closest guess.
problems.useAgain: when a whole structure is built from many identical small pieces and you can multiply rows by columns by sides.
hints: Think about how many bricks are in one row of one wall, not the whole house at once.
Multiply the bricks in one row by the rows in a wall, then by the number of walls.
problems.socraticHint: A brick wall has three separate things to estimate, not just two. Can you name all three before you multiply anything?

variant.prompt: About how many bricks make up one tall chimney?

problems.prompt: A 3D printer extrudes plastic at about 60 millimeters per minute. About how many meters of plastic does it extrude during an 8-hour print job?
explanation: Guess and round: 60 millimeters a minute is 3,600 millimeters, or 3.6 meters, in one hour.
Over an 8 hour print job, 3.6 x 8 is about 29 meters.
That rounds to about 30 meters of plastic total.
problems.useAgain: when a rate given in millimeters per minute needs to scale up to meters over several hours.
hints: Convert the rate to meters per hour first, before multiplying by the hours.
3,600 millimeters is the same as 3.6 meters.
problems.socraticHint: Is it easier to keep track of millimeters or to switch to meters partway through, once the numbers start growing?

variant.prompt: A 3D printer extrudes plastic at about 50 millimeters per minute. About how many meters of plastic does it extrude during a 6-hour print job?

problem.prompt: Write the letter p on paper, then turn the whole paper upside down (rotate it a full half turn). Which letter do you see now?
explanation: Turn it in your head: picture the whole letter spinning in a half turn, not flipped like in a mirror.
The letter p has its tall stroke on the left, going down below the line, and its round bowl on the right.
Turn it upside down. The down-going stroke on the left swings around to the right and now points up, and the bowl swings over to the left.
A tall stroke on the right going up, with the bowl on the left, is the letter d.
problem.useAgain: when a letter, shape or object is turned all the way around and you need to picture where each part ends up.
hints: Do not think of a mirror flip, think of spinning the whole page in a half circle.
Picture where the tall stroke and the round bowl each end up after the turn.
problem.socraticHint: If you actually wrote a p and spun the paper a half turn on your desk, would what you picture in your head match what the paper really shows?

figure.alt: The letter p, written upright, with a half turn shown by a curved arrow. The letter after the turn is not shown.

variant.prompt: Write the letter b on paper, then turn the whole paper upside down (rotate it a full half turn). Which letter do you see now?

figure.alt: The letter b, written upright, with a half turn shown by a curved arrow. The letter after the turn is not shown.

steps.title: Meet the idea: dividing by a fraction

explanationFigure.alt: Two bars, each cut into 6 equal pieces. The first bar has 4 shaded for 2 thirds, the second bar has 3 shaded for 1 half, the two fractions this problem divides by.

problems.prompt: Which of these equals 4 divided by 2/3, divided by 1/2?
explanation: Flip and multiply: work left to right, flipping each fraction you divide by.
4 divided by 2/3 is 4 x 3/2, which is 6.
6 divided by 1/2 is 6 x 2, which is 12.
problems.useAgain: when a problem chains two divisions by fractions in a row, one after the other.
hints: Do the two divisions one at a time, left to right, not all at once.
Flip each fraction upside down before multiplying, one step at a time.
problems.socraticHint: Dividing by a fraction smaller than one always makes a number bigger. After two such divisions, should the final answer be a lot bigger than 4, or just a little?

variant.prompt: Which of these equals 6 divided by 3/4, divided by 2?

explanationFigure.alt: Two bars, each cut into 8 equal pieces. The first bar is fully shaded for 1 whole, the second bar has 7 of its 8 pieces shaded, together showing the correct answer, 1 and 7 eighths.

problems.prompt:
Aisha found 3/4 divided by 2/5 like this:
Line 1: Flip and multiply: keep the first fraction the same and flip the second fraction upside down.
Line 2: Flip the first fraction instead: 3/4 becomes 4/3, and keep 2/5 the same.
Line 3: Multiply: 4/3 times 2/5 is 8/15.
Line 4: So 3/4 divided by 2/5 is 8/15.
Which line is wrong?
explanation: Line 2 is wrong: flip and multiply flips the second fraction, the one you are dividing by, not the first one.
Line 1 correctly states the rule, but line 2 applies it backwards.
Line 3's multiplication is done correctly for the numbers it uses, but those are the wrong numbers to multiply.
Flip the second fraction instead: 2/5 becomes 5/2. Then 3/4 times 5/2 is 15/8, which is 1 and 7/8.
problems.useAgain: when dividing by a fraction and deciding which fraction to flip upside down.
hints: Flip and multiply flips one specific fraction, the one right after the division. Which fraction got flipped here?
Check which fraction is being divided by, that is the one that should flip.
problems.socraticHint: Dividing by 2/5, a fraction less than one, should give a bigger answer than 3/4. Does 8/15 feel bigger or smaller than 3/4?

variant.prompt:
Carlos found 5/6 divided by 3/4 like this:
Line 1: Flip and multiply: keep the first fraction the same and flip the second fraction upside down.
Line 2: Flip the first fraction instead: 5/6 becomes 6/5, and keep 3/4 the same.
Line 3: Multiply: 6/5 times 3/4 is 18/20, which simplifies to 9/10.
Line 4: So 5/6 divided by 3/4 is 9/10.
Which line is wrong?

explanationFigure.alt: A grid of 3 rows and 4 columns, 12 squares total, with a 2 by 3 block of 6 squares shaded in the corner, showing that 3 quarters of 2 thirds is 6 out of 12 squares, or 1 half a cup.

problems.prompt: A recipe calls for 2/3 cup of flour for one batch. If you want to make 3/4 of a batch, how much flour do you need?
explanation: Of means times: 3/4 of a batch needs 3/4 of the flour for one full batch.
3/4 of 2/3 is 3/4 x 2/3, multiply straight across: 3x2 is 6, and 4x3 is 12.
6/12 simplifies to 1/2 cup of flour.
problems.useAgain: when you need a fraction of a batch, and the recipe amount is itself a fraction.
hints: Multiply the two fractions straight across, tops together and bottoms together.
Simplify the result at the end, since 6/12 is not in lowest terms.
problems.socraticHint: Is three quarters of two thirds of a cup more or less than half a cup, roughly?

variant.prompt: A recipe calls for 3/5 cup of sugar for one batch. If you want to make 2/3 of a batch, how much sugar do you need?

explanationFigure.alt: A grid of 3 rows and 4 columns, 12 squares total, with a 2 by 3 block of 6 squares shaded in the corner, showing that 2 thirds of 3 quarters is 6 out of 12 squares, or 1 half.

problems.prompt: Which of these equals 2/3 times 3/4?
explanation: Picture a chocolate bar cut into 3/4: that is three quarter-size slices out of the four the whole bar was cut into.
Now take 2/3 of that. Cut each of those three quarter-slices into 3 thin pieces, so the whole bar ends up cut into twelfths.
From each of the three quarter-slices, take 2 of its 3 thin pieces, since you want 2/3 of each quarter. 3 quarters times 2 pieces is 6 pieces out of twelve.
6 twelfths is 1/2 of the bar, the correct choice. Multiplying tops together and adding bottoms together, a common mix-up, would land on 6/7 instead.
problems.useAgain: when you multiply a fraction by another fraction, straight across, tops together and bottoms together.
hints: Multiply straight across: tops together, bottoms together.
Once you multiply straight across, check whether the top and bottom share a common factor to simplify.
problems.socraticHint: When you multiply two fractions that are each less than a whole, should the result be bigger or smaller than either one you started with?

variant.prompt: Which of these equals 3/4 times 2/5?

explanationFigure.alt: One bar cut into 8 equal pieces with 6 shaded, showing that 3 quarters is the same as 6 eighths, so 3 quarters divided by 1 eighth is 6.

problems.prompt: Which of these equals 3/4 divided by 1/8?
explanation: Flip and multiply: flip 1/8 upside down to get 8/1, then multiply instead of divide.
3/4 times 8 is 24/4.
24/4 simplifies to 6. Multiplying without flipping first, a common trap, gives 3/32 instead.
problems.useAgain: when you divide a fraction by another fraction and want to flip the second one before multiplying.
hints: Flip the second fraction upside down before multiplying.
Multiply the top number by the flipped whole number, then simplify what you get.
problems.socraticHint: Since eighths are smaller pieces than quarters, should dividing by an eighth give a bigger number or a smaller one than dividing by a quarter?

variant.prompt: Which of these equals 5/6 divided by 1/12?

problems.prompt: Which of these equals 2/3 divided by 3/5?
explanation: Flip and multiply: flip 3/5 upside down to get 5/3, then multiply instead of divide.
2/3 times 5/3 is 10/9, tops together and bottoms together.
10/9 is more than a whole, so rewrite it as 1 whole with 1/9 left over: 1 1/9. Flipping the wrong fraction gives 9/10.
problems.useAgain: when dividing two fractions gives an answer bigger than one whole and needs rewriting as a mixed number.
hints: Flip the second fraction before multiplying.
After multiplying, check whether the top number is bigger than the bottom.
problems.socraticHint: Just by comparing 2/3 and 3/5, before you flip and multiply anything, can you tell whether the result should be bigger or smaller than one whole?

variant.prompt: Which of these equals 3/4 divided by 2/3?

explanationFigure.alt: One bar cut into 6 equal pieces with 5 shaded, showing 5 sixths, the fraction taken of 24 in the first step of this problem.

problems.prompt: Which of these equals 5/6 times 24, divided by 2/3?
explanation: Of means times: 5/6 times 24 is the same as 5/6 of 24, which is 20.
Flip and multiply: dividing 20 by 2/3 means multiplying by 3/2.
20 times 3/2 is 30.
problems.useAgain: when a problem chains a fraction-of a number with a division by another fraction.
hints: Work out 5/6 of 24 completely first, before dividing by anything.
Flip 2/3 upside down and multiply instead of dividing.
problems.socraticHint: You already know two separate tricks, of means times, and flip and multiply. Does it matter which order you apply them in here, since they happen on different steps?

variant.prompt: Which of these equals 3/8 times 32, divided by 1/2?

explanationFigure.alt: One bar cut into 20 equal pieces with 3 shaded, showing that one check takes 3 out of 20 of a second.

problems.prompt: Suppose each line-follower check takes 0.15 seconds, which is 3/20 of a second. How many checks fit into 3 whole seconds?
explanation: This is 3 divided by 3/20, since you are asking how many 3/20-second checks fit into 3 whole seconds.
Flip and multiply: flip 3/20 upside down to get 20/3, then multiply instead of divide.
3 times 20/3 is 60/3, which simplifies to 20.
problems.useAgain: when a word problem asks how many equal fraction-sized portions fit into a whole amount.
hints: Turn the question into 3 divided by 3/20.
Flip 3/20 upside down before multiplying by 3.
problems.socraticHint: What question turns how many 3/20-second checks fit in 3 seconds into a division problem in the first place?

variant.prompt: Suppose each line-follower check takes 0.15 seconds, which is 3/20 of a second. How many checks fit into 6 whole seconds?

problems.prompt: A drawer has red, blue, green and yellow socks, many of each color. It is dark. How many socks must you pull out to be sure of a matching pair?
explanation: There are only four colors, so imagine four drawers, one per color.
Pull four socks and each one could land in a different color drawer, one each, with no pair yet.
Pull a fifth sock. There are only four drawers, so it must land where a sock already is. That is your pair.
problems.useAgain: when a question asks how many to be sure and there are fewer kinds of thing than things.
hints: Count the number of colors, not how many socks are in the drawer.
Imagine one drawer per color and drop socks in one at a time.
problems.socraticHint: If you pulled exactly one sock of every color, would you already have a matching pair?

variant.prompt: A drawer has red, blue and green socks, many of each color. How many socks must you pull out to be sure of a matching pair?

problems.prompt: A box has 3 sizes of hats, small, medium and large, many of each. How many hats must you pull out to be sure two are the same size?
explanation: There are only three sizes, so imagine three piles, one per size.
Pull three hats and each one could land in a different pile, one each, with no match yet.
Pull a fourth hat. There are only three piles, so it must land where a hat already is. That is your match.
problems.useAgain: when there are only a few categories and you need to guarantee two things land in the same one.
hints: Count the number of sizes, not how many hats are in the box.
Imagine one pile per size and drop hats in one at a time.
problems.socraticHint: How many separate piles would you need, one for each size, before you even start pulling a single hat?

variant.prompt: A box has 5 colors of gloves, many of each. How many gloves must you pull out to be sure two are the same color?

problems.prompt: A drawer has 10 red socks and 10 blue socks. It is dark. How many socks must you pull out to be sure of a matching pair?
explanation: There are only two colours. Think of two drawers: a red one and a blue one.
Pull one sock, it goes in one drawer. Pull a second, it might go in the other. Still no pair.
Pull a third sock. There are only two drawers, so it must land where a sock already is. That is your pair.
The 10 and 10 were a distraction. Only the number of colours matters.
problems.useAgain: when a question says how many to be sure and there are fewer kinds of thing than things.
hints: How many colours are there? Forget the tens.
Imagine one drawer per colour and drop socks in one at a time.
problems.socraticHint: Would the answer change at all if the drawer held 100 red socks and 100 blue ones instead of 10 of each? What does that tell you about which numbers in this problem actually matter?

variant.prompt: A bag has red, green and blue marbles, lots of each. Eyes closed, how many must you take to be sure of two the same colour?

problems.prompt: A class has 13 kids in it. There are 12 months in a year. Must at least two kids in the class share the same birth month?
explanation: Think of the 12 months as 12 boxes, one for each month.
If every kid had a different birth month, the most kids you could fit is 12, one per box.
There are 13 kids, one more than the 12 boxes, so at least one box must hold two kids.
That means at least two kids must share a birth month.
problems.useAgain: when there are more things than categories and you want to know if two things must land in the same category.
hints: Think of each month as a box that can hold kids.
Compare the number of kids to the number of boxes.
problems.socraticHint: If each of the 12 months could hold at most one kid with no repeats at all, how many kids would that use up?

variant.prompt: A class has 11 kids in it. There are 12 months in a year. Must at least two kids in the class share the same birth month?

problems.prompt: Five points are placed anywhere inside a square that is 2 units by 2 units. Prove that two of the points must be within about 1.5 units of each other.

mustMention: two points in the same small square

explanation: Cut the 2 by 2 square into four smaller squares, each 1 by 1, like a 2 by 2 grid of tiles.
There are 5 points and only 4 small squares, so by pigeonhole, at least one small square must contain two of the points.
The farthest apart two points can be inside one 1 by 1 square is the diagonal, corner to corner. That distance is about 1.4 units, a little less than 1.5.
So those two points, both inside the same small square, must be within about 1.5 units of each other.
problems.useAgain: when points or objects are spread inside a region and you want to guarantee two of them are close together.
hints: Cut the big square into four smaller equal squares, not into strips.
Think about the farthest two points can be apart inside just one small square.
problems.socraticHint: Why cut the square into four equal pieces instead of, say, five thin strips?

problems.prompt: A city has 900,000 people living in it. No person has more than 200,000 hairs on their head. Prove that at least two people in the city have the exact same number of hairs on their head.

mustMention: more people than possible hair counts
two people share the same count

explanation: Think of every possible hair count from 0 to 200,000 as a box, which is 200,001 boxes in total.
There are 900,000 people, far more than the number of boxes.
By pigeonhole, if there are more people than boxes, at least one box must hold more than one person.
That box represents one exact hair count, so at least two people in the city share that exact same number of hairs.
problems.useAgain: when there are more people or things than the number of possible values something can take, and you want to guarantee two match exactly.
hints: Think of every possible hair count as its own box.
Compare how many boxes there are to how many people there are.
problems.socraticHint: How many different hair-count values are even possible, counting from zero up to the highest anyone could have?

problems.prompt: A bag has jellybeans in 6 flavors, plenty of each. How many jellybeans must you pull out to be sure that 3 of them are the same flavor?
explanation: This time you need three of a kind, not just a pair, so one per drawer is not enough to avoid a match.
Imagine six drawers, one per flavor. You could pull two jellybeans into every drawer, 2 times 6 is 12, with no drawer holding three yet.
Pull one more jellybean, the thirteenth. There are only six drawers, and each already holds two, so this one pushes some drawer to three.
13 jellybeans guarantees three of the same flavor.
problems.useAgain: when a question asks for more than a pair, like three or four of the same kind, and you want to fill every category almost full first.
hints: Think about filling every flavor drawer with two jellybeans before a third shows up anywhere.
Imagine the unluckiest picking: how many can you take before any flavor has three?
problems.socraticHint: Why does needing three matching, instead of just two, let you fill every flavor further before anything has to repeat?

variant.prompt: A bag has marbles in 4 colors, plenty of each. How many marbles must you pull out to be sure that 3 of them are the same color?

problems.prompt: A triangle has two angles measuring 55 degrees and 80 degrees. What is the third angle, in degrees?
explanation: A triangle's three angles always add up to 180 degrees.
Add the two known angles: 55 plus 80 is 135.
180 minus 135 is 45 degrees.
problems.useAgain: when two of a triangle's three angles are known and the third is missing.
hints: What do all three angles of a triangle add up to?
Add the two known angles, then subtract that from 180.
problems.socraticHint: If you tore off all three corners of any triangle and lined them up, what shape would they always make together?

variant.prompt: A triangle has two angles measuring 60 degrees and 70 degrees. What is the third angle, in degrees?

problems.prompt: A fair six-sided die is rolled once. What is the probability, as a fraction, of rolling a number greater than 4?
explanation: The numbers greater than 4 on a die are 5 and 6, which is 2 out of the 6 faces.
2 out of 6 simplifies to 1/3.
problems.useAgain: when a die's probability rule is a range of numbers, like greater than a certain value.
hints: Which numbers on the die are greater than 4?
Count those faces and put that count over 6, then simplify.
problems.socraticHint: Does greater than 4 include the number 4 itself?

variant.prompt: A fair six-sided die is rolled once. What is the probability, as a fraction, of rolling a 6?

steps.title: Explain it in writing
steps.prompt: Write, in your own words, why three socks is always enough to guarantee a matching pair.

steps.title: Explain it out loud
steps.prompt: Record yourself explaining why the answer works, and say what would change if there were three colours instead of two.
